messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Seventeen months after the assault, 27‑year‑old Nabil, a Middle Eastern physical therapist, found himself on the brink of collapse. The night of the incident, he was a junior resident at a downtown bar, laughing with classmates when a friend’s cologne—an unmistakable amber‑scented fragrance—warmed his nostrils. In a moment of drunken abandon, a fellow student grabbed him, pressed his body into a painful, unnatural posture, and forcefully pressed his mouth to his chest. The pain lodged deep in Nabil’s back, and the intimate, violent touch left his skin raw and shameful. The next morning, while helping a client lift a limb, the slightest ache in his lower back felt like a flashback; his wife’s soft kiss during a quiet evening felt like an invasion. The smell of his own cologne, the physical sting of a misaligned vertebra during a routine stretch, and the mere possibility of sexual intimacy became unmistakable triggers. The first time the cologne hit his nose, Nabil’s mind flooded with the words he had been forced to hear during the assault: “I cannot trust my body.” He began to interpret every scent, every jolt of pain, as a reminder that he would never again feel normal emotions. He declared to himself, “I will never be able to feel normal emotions again.” The memory of the assault convinced him that he could not rely on himself; he could not rely on his own bodily sensations or his own judgment. The shame he carried—“I feel ashamed of what happened to my body”—deepened his belief that the world had turned against him. In this way, the triggers did not simply elicit memory; they amplified his negative appraisals, which in turn made the same smells, pains, and intimacy even more unbearable. The scent of that particular cologne, the slightest pressure on his back, and any hint of intimacy became the very cues that pulled his negative appraisals to the surface. Nabil’s negative appraisals carried him into a constant state of threat. He perceived the office’s fluorescent lights, the receptionist’s casual touch, and even the gentle sway of a chair as potential dangers. A sudden clatter of a coffee mug would send his heart racing, as if a predator were nearby. The sense that “I can’t rely on myself” made every touch—a client’s hand on his arm, a colleague’s brief pat—trigger a startle response. The startle to touch made him react with alarm at any unexpected contact, while the startle to movement made him jump whenever a patient shifted. These threat perceptions intensified his hypervigilance. Threat, in turn, pushed him into maladaptive strategies. When a client reached out for a stretch, Nabil would pull back, pretending the assault had happened to someone else, and mentally distance himself. He avoided thinking about the event altogether, and he spent hours checking his body for pain, as if any sign of discomfort could signal imminent danger. Threat also amplified the triggers: a whiff of a new cologne in the waiting room could feel like the scent that had once trapped him, and a mild ache in his elbow could feel as if his back had been struck again. The maladaptive strategies Nabil employed fed back into the loop. Dissociating—pretending the assault had happened to another—only deepened his detachment from his own body, so the slightest contact or ache felt more threatening. Avoiding thoughts of the event left the memory vivid, so any trigger could ignite a flood of negative appraisal. Body monitoring heightened his perception of danger, turning even a routine check of his joints into a potential trigger. Each time he avoided the thought of the assault, he was left to confront the triggers alone, which intensified his sense of threat. Maladaptive strategies, in turn, fed back into threat, making his startle responses more intense whenever a new scent, pain, or intimacy arose. The cycle tightened, leaving Nabil feeling as if he were walking a tightrope of fear that could snap at any moment. After months of living in this state—waking each day with a racing heart, feeling the receptionist’s light touch like a betrayal, and being unable to touch a patient’s back without the flashback—Nabil finally sought help. He feared that if he did not break the loop, his marriage would dissolve because intimacy remained a source of terror, and his ability to serve patients would erode. He wanted to regain the normal emotions he felt were lost, to trust his own body again, and to restore a sense of safety in the very places that once sparked terror. The hope that therapy could pull him out of the self‑reinforcing cycle of threat, triggers, and maladaptive strategies became the driving force behind his decision to seek treatment.
